title: TRIVENI SHIVHARE versus SANJAY VYAS   Advocate- ,KUSH GOSWAMI 1123

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
THE HON'BLE SRI JUSTICE SIDDHARTHA SAH
09th OCTOBER, 2026
CIVIL REVISION NO. 142 OF 2026
Smt. Triveni Shivhare and Another .....Revisionists
Versus
Sanjay Vyas ......Respondent
Counsel for the Revisionists : Mr. Tapan Singh, learned
Counsel.
Counsel for the Respondent : Mr. Piyush Garg, Learned
Senior Counsel assisted by
Mr. Raghav Singhal, learned
counsel.
Hon'ble Siddhartha Sah, J. (Oral)
By means of the present civil revision, filed
under Section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts
Act, 1887, the defendants/revisionists has sought
setting aside/ quashing of the impugned order dated
17.09.2026, passed by learned First Additional District
Judge, Rishikesh, District Dehradun in SCC Suit No.7 of
2023, "Shri Sanjay Vyas Vs. Triveni Shivhare &
another", by means of which the amendment
application bearing paper no.53C filed by the
1

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
defendants/ revisionists for amendment in the their
written statement has been rejected.
Admit.
2. Facts necessary for adjudication of the
present civil revision are as under:
(a) The respondent has filed a SCC suit,
bearing SCC Suit No.41 of 2023 before the
learned First Additional District Judge,
Rishikesh, Dehradun against the defendants/
revisionists for decree of eviction and recovery
of arrears of rent.
(b) The defendants/revisionists contested the
said SCC suit by filing the written statement
denying and disputing the averments made in
the plaint. A replica was also filed by the
plaintiff. The plaintiff / respondent filed his
affidavit in examination-in-chief before the trial
court, and he was cross-examined by the
counsel for the defendants/revisionists.
(c) It is the case of the
defendants/revisionists that during the
adjudication of the present case, it came to
their knowledge that there are some clerical
2

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
errors in their written statements, and some
important facts in the written statement were
required to be added in the written
statement, therefore, an amendment
application was filed under Order VI Rule 17
of the CPC to seek certain amendments in the
written statement.
(d) The plaintiff/respondent filed his
objection to the amendment application
seeking rejection of the amendment
application.
(e) By the impugned order dated
17.09.2026, the trial court rejected the
amendment application, hence, the present
civil revision.
3. Assailing the impugned order dated
17.09.2026, learned counsel for the defendants /
revisionists would submit that the judgment relied upon
in paragraph 8 of the impugned order pertains to
amendment in the plaint and, therefore, the learned
First Additional District Judge, Rishikesh, Dehradun has
erred by relying upon the said judgment and rejecting
3

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
the amendment application preferred by the defendants
/ revisionists.
4. Learned counsel for the defendants /
revisionists has relied upon judgment of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in the case of Usha Balashaheb
Swami & Ors. Vs. Kiran Appaso Swami & Ors.
reported in (2007) 5 SCC 602 and has relied upon its
paragraph nos.19 to 26 and he would submit that for
addition of a new ground of defense or substituting or
altering a defense or taking inconsistent pleas in the
written statement would not be objectionable, while
adding, altering, or substituting a new cause of action
in the plaint may be objectionable. He would further
submit that it is settled law that, in the case of
amendment of a written statement, the Courts are
more liberal in allowing an amendment than that of a
plaint, as the question of prejudice would be far less in
the former than in the latter case. Para 19 to 26 in the
case of Usha Balashaheb Swami & Ors. Vs. Kiran
Appaso Swami & Ors.(Supra) are being extracted
hereunder for ready reference:
"19. It is equally well-settled principle that a
prayer for amendment of the plaint and a prayer for
amendment of the written statement stand on
4

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
different footings. The general principle that
amendment of pleadings cannot be allowed so as to
alter materially or substitute cause of action or the
nature of claim applies to amendments to plaint. It
has no counterpart in the principles relating to
amendment of the written statement. Therefore,
addition of a new ground of defence or substituting
or altering a defence or taking inconsistent pleas in
the written statement would not be objectionable
while adding, altering or substituting a new cause of
action in the plaint may be objectionable.
20. Such being the settled law, we must hold that
in the case of amendment of a written statement,
the courts are more liberal in allowing an
amendment than that of a plaint as the question of
prejudice would be far less in the former than in the
latter case (see B.K. Narayana Pillai v.
Parameswaran Pillai [(2000) 1 SCC 712] and Baldev
Singh v. Manohar Singh [(2006) 6 SCC 498] ). Even
the decision relied on by the plaintiff in Modi Spg.
[(1976) 4 SCC 320] clearly recognises that
inconsistent pleas can be taken in the pleadings. In
this context, we may also refer to the decision of this
Court in Basavan Jaggu Dhobi v. Sukhnandan
Ramdas Chaudhary [1995 Supp (3) SCC 179] . In
that case, the defendant had initially taken up the
stand that he was a joint tenant along with others.
Subsequently, he submitted that he was a licensee
for monetary consideration who was deemed to be a
tenant as per the provisions of Section 15-A of the
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates
Control Act, 1947. This Court held that the defendant
could have validly taken such an inconsistent
defence. While allowing the amendment of the
written statement, this Court observed in Basavan
Jaggu Dhobi case [1995 Supp (3) SCC 179] as
follows: (SCC p. 180, para 3)
"3. As regards the first contention, we are
afraid that the courts below have gone wrong in
holding that it is not open to the defendant to
amend his written statement under Order 6 Rule
17 CPC by taking a contrary stand than what was
stated originally in the written statement. This is
opposed to the settled law. It is open to a
defendant to take even contrary stands or
contradictory stands, thereby the cause of action
is not in any manner affected. That will apply only
to a case of the plaint being amended so as to
introduce a new cause of action."
21. As we have already noted herein earlier that
in allowing the amendment of the written statement
a liberal approach is a general view when admittedly
in the event of allowing the amendment the other
5

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
party can be compensated in money. Technicality of
law should not be permitted to hamper the courts in
the administration of justice between the parties. In
L.J. Leach & Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner & Co. [AIR
1957 SC 357] this Court observed
"that the courts are more generous in allowing
amendment of the written statement as the
question of prejudice is less likely to operate in
that event".
In that case this Court also held
"that the defendant has right to take alternative
plea in defence which, however, is subject to an
exception that by the proposed amendment the
other side should not be subjected to serious
injustice".
22. Keeping these principles in mind, namely,
that in a case of amendment of a written statement
the courts would be more liberal in allowing than that
of a plaint as the question of prejudice would be far
less in the former than in the latter and addition of a
new ground of defence or substituting or altering a
defence or taking inconsistent pleas in the written
statement can also be allowed, we may now proceed
to consider whether the High Court was justified in
rejecting the application for amendment of the
written statement.
23. As noted herein earlier, Mr Lalit placed strong
reliance on Heeralal [(1998) 1 SCC 278] to contend
that the admission made by the appellants in the
original written statement in the facts and
circumstances of the case could not at all be taken
away. In our view, the factual position of the case
before us and the facts involved in that decision are
different. In Heeralal case [(1998) 1 SCC 278] a
definite stand was taken that the plaintiff had a share
in seven out of the ten scheduled properties as they
belonged to the plaintiff and Defendants 1 and 2 as
joint family properties. However, the defendants
moved an application for amendment of the written
statement, which was not allowed by the trial court.
While dealing with this nature of amendment, in that
decision, this Court observed that it was wrong on
the part of the High Court to assume that by taking
an inconsistent stand, the respondents would
prejudicially affect the appellant's case. The Court
observed: (SCC pp. 281-82, para 6)
"6. In our view, the order passed by the High
Court under Section 115 CPC, allowing withdrawal
of earlier admissions of Defendants 1 and 2 in
their original written statement about 5 out of 7
items of Schedule A properties cannot be
sustained. The reason is obvious. So far as
6

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
Schedule A properties were concerned, a clear
admission was made by Defendants 1 and 2 in
their joint written statement in 1993 that 7
properties out of 10 were joint family properties
wherein the plaintiff had 1/3rd share and they had
2/3rds undivided share. Once such a stand was
taken, naturally it must be held that there was no
contest between the parties regarding 7 items of
suit properties in Schedule A. The learned trial
Judge, therefore, was perfectly justified in framing
Issue 2 concerning only remaining three items for
which there was dispute between the parties. In
such a situation under Order 15 Rule 1 CPC the
plaintiff even would have been justified in
requesting the court to pass a preliminary decree
forthwith qua these 7 properties. The said
provision lays down that, 'where at the first
hearing of a suit it appears that the parties are
not at issue on any question of law or of fact, the
Court may at once pronounce the judgment'. Even
that apart, the defendant-respondents did not
think it fit to move any amendment application for
getting out of such admission till the plaintiff
moved an application for appointment of receiver
regarding admitted items of properties. It is only
thereafter that the application for amendment was
moved. Learned trial Judge was right when he
observed that even the grounds made out in the
application were not justified. Consequently, there
is no question of taking inconsistent stand which
would not have affected prejudicially the plaintiff
as wrongly assumed by the High Court."
Keeping the aforesaid observations and also the facts
involved in Heeralal case [(1998) 1 SCC 278] in
mind, we are of the view that the decision in that
case may not be of any help to the respondents.
24. Coming back to the facts of the present case
regarding amendment of the written statement, we
find that the appellants had stated in para 8 of their
original written statement "that the plaintiff and
Defendants 1 to 7 have got 1⁄2 share and Defendants
8 to 14 have got 1⁄2 share in all the family properties"
and that the maternal aunts have also got share. By
seeking incorporation of paras 8-A and 8-B and
substitution of para 8 in the written statement, the
appellants have maintained the admissions made by
them in para 8 of the written statement but added a
proviso or condition to the admission. Therefore, it
was not a case of withdrawal of the admission by the
appellants by making the application for the
amendment of the written statement but in fact such
admission was kept intact and only a proviso has
been added. This, in our view, is permissible in law
7

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
and the question of withdrawing the admission made
in para 8 in its entirety in the facts as noted
hereinabove, therefore, cannot arise at all.
25. Since we have already held that in the case of
amendment of a written statement, the defendant is
entitled to take new defence and also to plead
inconsistent stand and in view of our discussions
made hereinabove that by making the application for
amendment of the written statement, admission was
not at all withdrawn by the appellants nor a totally
inconsistent plea was taken by the appellants in their
application for amendment of the written statement,
the High Court had failed to appreciate that by the
proposed amendment, the appellants were not
withdrawing their admission in respect of the half-share in the ancestral property rather they only
added that the plaintiff and Defendants 3 to 8 could
be entitled to such share if they proved to be the
legitimate children of Appasao (since deceased) who
was entitled to half-share in the property of late
Veersangayya. That apart, it appears from the record
that the written statement filed by the appellants
was before the death of Defendant 1 (first wife of
Appasao). After the death of Defendant 1, when the
plaintiff and Defendants 2 to 8 claimed themselves
as heirs and legal representatives of Defendant 1,
the appellants sought amendment of the written
statement challenging the legitimacy of the plaintiff
and Defendants 2 to 8. In view of the discussions
made hereinabove, we do not think that it was
impermissible in law for the appellants to seek
amendment of the written statement in the manner
it was sought for.
26. Therefore, it was neither a case of withdrawal
of admission made in the written statement nor a
case of washing out admission made by the appellant
in the written statement. As noted herein earlier, by
such amendment the appellant had kept the
admissions intact and only added certain additional
facts which need to be proved by the plaintiff and
Defendants 2 to 8 to get shares in the suit properties
alleged to have been admitted by the appellants in
their written statement. Accordingly, we are of the
view that the appellants are only raising an issue
regarding the legitimacy of the plaintiff and
Defendants 3 to 7 to inherit the suit properties as
heirs and legal representatives of the deceased
Appasao. Therefore, it must be held that in view of
our discussions made hereinabove, the High Court
was not justified in reversing the order of the trial
court and rejecting the application for amendment of
the written statement."
8

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
5. Per contra, learned Senior Counsel for the
plaintiff/ respondent would submit that the defendant
no.1 is also a tenant. An agreement was executed by
the defendant no.1 for the tenancy. By virtue of the
amendment being sought, the defendants are
withdrawing the admission that defendant no.1 is also
a tenant. Learned Senior Counsel for the
plaintiff/respondent has drawn the attention of the
Court to a judgment rendered by a Coordinate bench of
this Court in Civil Revision No.56 of 2026, "Triveni
Shivhare and Another Vs. Sanjay Vyas" dated
09.09.2026 and has drawn the attention to para no.15
thereof, which is being extracted here under for ready
reference:-
"15. This court is in agreement with the view taken
by the learned Trial Court that the said Trust was not
a necessary party to the suit, as there exists the
relationship of landlord and tenant between the
parties, and as such, there is no illegality or
perversity in the said order."
6. Learned Senior Counsel for the plaintiff/
respondent would submit that in para no.15 of the
judgment dated 09.09.2026, the Co-ordinate Bench of
this Court has given a clear finding about the
relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties,
therefore, there is no scope for the
9

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
defendants/revisionists to resile from that finding, since
the said finding has attained finality.
7. Learned Senior Counsel would further submit
that the agreement between the plaintiff /respondent
and defendants/revisionists is a part of the record of
the trial court in which the defendant no.1, Triveni
Shivhare, is a second party /tenant. Learned counsel
for the plaintiff/respondent has also drawn the
attention of this court to the amendment being sought
by way of the amendment application, which is para ".k"
of the proposed amendment, which has been quoted
here under for ready reference:
"1⁄4.k1⁄2& ;g fd çfrokn i= d s vfrfjä dFku 'kh"kZd d s vUrxZr pj.k
l a[;k 31 dh f}rh; ifä esa "ugh gS" ds i'pkr ~ fuEu çdkj tksMk
tk;s&
"rFkk ;g Li"V fd;k tkrk gS fd çfroknh lå 1 dHkh Hkh oknxzlr
lEifÙk esa fdjk;snkj] v/;kflr ugh jghA"
8. Learned Senior Counsel for the
plaintiff/respondent would further submit that the
amendment sought is hit by proviso to Order 6 Rule 17
of the CPC.
9. Learned counsel for the plaintiff/respondent
has further relied upon the judgment of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in Heeralal Vs. Kalyan Mal and
Others reported in (1998) 1 Supreme Court
10

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
Cases 278 and has relied upon para 6, 10,11 and 12,
which have been extracted hereunder for ready
reference:
"6. In our view, the order passed by the High
Court under Section 115 CPC, allowing withdrawal of
earlier admissions of Defendants 1 and 2 in their
original written statement about 5 out of 7 items of
Schedule A properties cannot be sustained. The
reason is obvious. So far as Schedule A properties
were concerned, a clear admission was made by
Defendants 1 and 2 in their joint written statement in
1993 that 7 properties out of 10 were joint family
properties wherein the plaintiff had 1/3rd share and
they had 2/3rds undivided share. Once such a stand
was taken, naturally it must be held that there was
no contest between the parties regarding 7 items of
suit properties in Schedule A. The learned trial Judge,
therefore, was perfectly justified in framing Issue No.
2 concerning only remaining three items for which
there was dispute between the parties. In such a
situation under Order XV Rule 1 of CPC the plaintiff
even would have been justified in requesting the
Court to pass a preliminary decree forthwith qua
these 7 properties. The said provision lays down
that, "where at the first hearing of a suit it appears
that the parties are not at issue on any question of
law or of fact, the Court may at once pronounce the
judgment". Even that apart, the defendant-respondents did not think it fit to move any
amendment application for getting out of such
admission till the plaintiff moved an application for
appointment of receiver regarding admitted items of
properties. It is only thereafter that the application
for amendment was moved. Learned trial Judge was
right when he observed that even the grounds made
out in the application were not justified.
Consequently, there is no question of taking
inconsistent stand which would not have affected
prejudicially the plaintiff as wrongly assumed by the
High Court. We also fail to appreciate how the
decisions on which strong reliance was placed by the
learned counsel for the respondents can be of any
assistance to him. We may briefly refer to them.
7.....
8.....
9....
10. Consequently it must be held that when the
amendment sought in the written statement was of
11

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
such a nature as to displace the plaintiff's case it
could not be allowed as ruled by a three-member
Bench of this Court. This aspect was unfortunately
not considered by the latter Bench of two learned
Judges and to the extent to which the latter decision
took a contrary view qua such admission in written
statement, it must be held that it was per incuriam
being rendered without being given an opportunity to
consider the binding decision of a three-member
Bench of this Court taking a diametrically opposite
view.
11. We were then taken to another decision of
this Court in the case of Panchdeo Narain Srivastava
v. Jyoti Sahay [1984 Supp SCC 594] . In that case
the plaintiff was held entitled to amend his plaint by
submitting that though earlier he stated that the
defendant was uterine brother, the plaintiff by
amendment in his plaint could submit that the
defendant was his brother and the word "uterine"
could be dropped. Even in that case the main case
put forward by the plaintiff did not get changed as
the plaintiff wanted to submit that the defendant was
his brother. Whether he was uterine brother or real
brother was a question of decree and depended on
the nature of evidence that may be led before the
Court. Therefore, the deletion of the word "uterine"
was not found to be displacing the earlier case of the
plaintiff. On the facts of the present case also,
therefore, the said decision cannot be of any
assistance to the learned counsel for the
respondents.
12. In our view, therefore, on the facts of this
case and as discussed earlier, no case was made out
by the respondents, contesting defendants, for
amending the written statement and thus attempting
to go behind their admission regarding 5 out of 7
remaining items out of 10 listed properties in
Schedule A of the plaint. However, so far as Schedule
B properties are concerned, from the very inception
the defendants' case qua those properties was that
the plaintiff had no interest therein. By proposed
amendment they wanted to introduce an event with
reference to those very properties by submitting that
they had been in possession of trespassers. Such
amendment could not be said to have in any way
adversely or prejudicially affected the case of the
plaintiff or displaced any admission on their part qua
Schedule B properties which might have resulted into
any legal right in favour of the plaintiff. Therefore, so
far as Schedule B properties were concerned, the
amendment could not be found fault with. Hence
exercising the powers under Article 136 of the
Constitution of India we would not be inclined to
12

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
interfere with that part of the decision of the High
Court allowing the amendment in the written
statement, even though strictly speaking High Court
could not have interfered with even this part of the
order under Section 115 CPC."
10. Learned Senior Counsel for the
plaintiff/respondent while placing reliance on the
aforesaid judgment Heeralal (supra) would submit
that it is settled law that withdrawal of the earlier
admission is not permissible. He would further submit
that when the amendment sought in the written
statement was of such a nature as to displace the
plaintiff's case it could not be allowed.
11. Learned Senior Counsel for the plaintiff/
respondent has also relied upon the judgment of
the Hon'ble Supreme Court in M/s Modi Spinning
& Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. and Another Vs. M/s
Lodha Ram & Co. reported in (1976) 4 SCC 320
and has drawn attention of this Court to para 9 and 10
thereof and he would submit that it is settled law that
defendants cannot be allowed to change completely the
case and substitute an entirely different and new case.
It is also a settled law that though inconsistent pleas
can be taken but the effect of amendment should not
be to displace the plaintiff completely from the
13

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
admissions made by the defendants in the written
statement. Para 9 and 10 thereof are being extracted
hereunder for ready reference:
"9. The decision of the trial court is correct. The
defendants cannot be allowed to change completely
the case made in paras 25 and 26 of the written
statement and substitute an entirely different and
new case.
10. It is true that inconsistent pleas can be made
in pleadings but the effect of substitution of paras 25
and 26 is not making inconsistent and alternative
pleadings but it is seeking to displace the plaintiff
completely from the admissions made by the
defendants in the written statement. If such
amendments are allowed the plaintiff will be
irretrievably prejudiced by being denied the
opportunity of extracting the admission from the
defendants. The High Court rightly rejected the
application for amendment and agreed with the trial
court."
12. He would lastly, submit that the stage at
which the amendment was sought to be made in the
written statement is stage of cross-examination of the
defendant. He would thus submit that at this stage the
amendment application under Order VI Rule 17 of the
CPC can be allowed provided due diligence can be
shown by a party.
13. Heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the record.
14. After going through the record, the two key
points come up for determination in this case as under:
14

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
i) Whether the amendment sought in the
written statement was in the nature of
withdrawing of earlier admission?
ii) Whether the amendment being sought in
the written statement was hit by proviso to
Order 6 Rule 17 of the CPC?
15. Point for determination no.i) - Perusal of
the proposed amendment would reveal that what is
being materially sought by virtue of the amendment is
that the defendant wanted to clarify by virtue of the
amendment that defendant no.1 has never been tenant
/occupant in the disputed property.
16. Learned counsel for the defendants/
revisionists would submit that initially in the written
statement there was an error which needed to be
rectified by amendment sought in para '.k' and,
therefore, it would not be hit by proviso to Order 6 Rule
17 of the CPC and there were certain legal course as
well.
17. On the other hand, learned Senior Counsel
for the plaintiff/respondent would submit that
defendant no.1 is also a tenant and there was an
agreement executed by defendant no.1 and in para
15

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
no.19 of the additional pleas of the written statement
there was clear admission that the defendant had taken
the establishment in question in the year 2012 which
was deemed to be in the ownership of the plaintiff. It is
also argued that in a prior civil revision no.56 of 2026 a
finding has been returned by the Co-ordinate Bench of
this Court about the landlord-tenant relationship
between the parties and the agreement is also part of
the record. In such circumstances, para '.k' by virtue of
which the defendant wanted to seek an amendment
that defendant no.1 had never been tenant in
occupation of the disputed property would thus be
withdrawal of the admission. It is settled law in the
cases of Modi Spinning (supra) and Heera Lal
(supra) that withdrawal of admission in pleadings is
not admissible.
18. In such view of the matter, the point for
determination no.(i) is decided to the effect that the
defendants/ revisionists by virtue of the proposed
amendment were desirous of withdrawal of the
admission and the trial court has returned the finding
that the proposed amendment is not merely a clerical
error but from the proposed amendment the very
16

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
nature of the plaint would change. Therefore, the
amendment sought in the written statement would be
withdrawing an earlier admission. Therefore, no error is
found in the finding returned by the First Additional
District Judge, Rishikesh, Dehradun to this effect.
Therefore, point for determination no.i) is answered
against the defendants / revisionists.
19. Point for determination no.ii) - On one
hand, the learned counsel for the defendants/
revisionists would submit that the trial court has
wrongly relied upon the judgment of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in para 8 about the amendment was
not permissible after the commencement of trial and he
would submit that the judgment of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in the case of J. Samuel and Others
Vs. Gattu Mahesh and Others (2012) 2 SCC 300
was in the matter of amendment in the plaint and that
the trial court could not have relied upon it when the
amendment is sought in the written statement.
20. On the other hand, learned counsel for the
plaintiff/ respondent would submit that the stage at
which the amendment was sought in the written
statement was when the examination-in-chief of the
17

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
defendant was already complete and it was at the stage
of cross-examination of the defendants/ revisionists,
therefore, the amendment sought by the defendants/
revisionists is clearly hit by proviso to Order 6 Rule 17
of the CPC. In this regard, learned Senior Counsel
would further submit that though amendment either in
plaint or the written statement needs to be liberally
allowed, but this would not mean that it would be a
free play and amendment can be allowed at any stage.
In the case of Ajendraprasadji N.Pandey and
Another Vs. Swami Keshavprakeshdasji N. and
Others reported in (2006) 12 SCC 1 the Hon'ble
Supreme Court has clearly held for seeking amendment
in the pleadings post commencement of trial, due
diligence has to be shown by the party seeking
amendment. In this context reference needs to be
made to para 55 of the case of Ajendraprasadji
(supra) which is being extracted hereunder for ready
reference:
"55. We have carefully perused the pleadings and
grounds which are raised in the amendment
application preferred by the appellants at Ext. 95. No
facts are pleaded nor are any grounds raised in the
amendment application to even remotely contend
that despite exercise of due diligence these matters
could not be raised by the appellants. Under these
circumstances, the case is covered by proviso to Rule
17 of Order 6 and, therefore, the relief deserves to
18

UKHC010175372026
2026:UHC:9211
be denied. The grant of amendment at this belated
stage when deposition and evidence of three
witnesses is already over as well as the documentary
evidence is already tendered, coupled with the fact
that the appellants' application at Ext. 64 praying for
recasting of the issues having been denied and the
said order never having been challenged by the
appellants, the grant of the present amendment as
sought for at this stage of the proceedings would
cause serious prejudice to the contesting
respondent-original plaintiffs and hence it is in the
interest of justice that the amendment sought for be
denied and the petition be dismissed."
21. In the present case, due diligence has also
not been shown by the defendants/ revisionists as
much as the relationship between the landlord and
tenant has already attained finality by virtue of
judgment dated 09.09.2026 rendered by Co-ordinate
Bench of this Court.
22. In such view of the matter, the submission as
advanced by learned counsel for the defendants/
revisionists that the judgment has been wrongly relied
upon by the trial court regarding the amendment does
not find favour with the Court. In such view of the
matter since the amendment was at the very belated
stage i.e. at the stage of cross-examination of the
